name: Scandium oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real crystal is the cubic bixbyite type.

bonding.summary: Sc3+ and O2− ions in the cubic bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Each scandium gives all three valence electrons to oxygen.

occurrence: Recovered from uranium, titanium and rare-earth processing.
uses: Electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells
facts: World scandium supply is only tens of tonnes a year.
summary: Scandia is a very high-melting oxide that feeds scandium alloys and fuel cells.

name: Yttrium oxide

bonding.summary: Y3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Yttrium gives three electrons to oxygen.

facts: Europium-doped yttria made the red dots in color TV screens.
summary: Yttria is the host crystal for many phosphors and stabilizes zirconia.

name: Lanthanum oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real crystal is hexagonal (A-type).

bonding.summary: Large La3+ ions with seven oxygen neighbors.
bonding.electronSharing: Lanthanum gives three electrons to oxygen.

uses: High-refractive optical glass for camera lenses
facts: Many high-end camera lenses contain glass that is up to 40% lanthanum oxide.
summary: Lanthanum oxide gives optical glass a high refractive index.

name: Praseodymium(III,IV) oxide

bonding.summary: A mixed-valence oxide: four Pr4+ and two Pr3+ per eleven oxygens.
bonding.electronSharing: Most praseodymium atoms give four electrons, some three, so oxygen vacancies form in a fluorite-like lattice.

formation: Heating praseodymium salts in air above about 500 °C
facts: It is the stable dark-brown oxide that forms when praseodymium burns in air.
summary: Pr6O11 is a mixed-valence oxide behind the bright yellow of many ceramic glazes.

name: Europium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Eu3+ and O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Europium gives three electrons. Its remaining 4f electrons jump between levels and emit sharp red light.

uses: Red phosphors for screens and lamps
facts: Europium's red glow has an unusually narrow color band, which is ideal for displays.
summary: Europium oxide is the source of the pure red glow in displays.

name: Gadolinium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Gd3+ and O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Gadolinium gives three electrons and keeps a half-filled 4f7 shell with seven unpaired electrons.

uses: Burnable neutron absorber mixed into nuclear fuel
facts: Adding Gd2O3 to fuel pellets evens out reactor power early in a fuel cycle.
summary: Gadolinia soaks up neutrons inside nuclear fuel.

name: Holmium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Ho3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Holmium gives three electrons; its 4f electrons absorb light at very sharp, well-known wavelengths.

uses: Yellow and red colorant for glass and cubic zirconia
facts: Holmium oxide looks tan in daylight but pink under fluorescent light.
summary: Holmia's sharp absorption lines make it a calibration standard.

name: Erbium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Er3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Erbium gives three electrons; its 4f electrons absorb green light, so the oxide is pink.

uses: Pink colorant for glass and porcelain
facts: Erbium-colored glass is used in some sunglasses and cheap jewelry for its pink tint.
summary: Erbia is a pink oxide that colors glass.

name: Thulium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Tm3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Thulium gives three electrons to oxygen.

uses: Target for making thulium-170 X-ray sources
facts: Irradiated thulium oxide makes portable X-ray sources that need no electricity.
summary: Thulia is the precursor to portable thulium-170 X-ray sources.

name: Ytterbium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Yb3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Ytterbium gives three electrons to oxygen.

facts: Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers are among the most efficient high-power lasers.
summary: Ytterbia is the raw material for ytterbium laser crystals and fibers.

name: Lutetium(III) oxide

bonding.summary: Lu3+ and O2− ions in the bixbyite structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Lutetium gives three electrons, leaving a full 4f14 shell.

uses: Making LYSO scintillator crystals for PET scanners
facts: Lutetium-based crystals detect the gamma rays in most modern PET scanners.
summary: Lutetia is the basis of the scintillator crystals in PET scanners.

name: Hafnium dioxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real hafnia is monoclinic like zirconia.

bonding.summary: Hf4+ and O2− in a monoclinic structure, like zirconia.
bonding.electronSharing: Hafnium gives four electrons toward oxygen; the highly polarizable bonds give it a high dielectric constant.

formation: HfCl4 + 2 H2O -> HfO2 + 4 HCl (atomic layer deposition)
uses: High-k gate insulator in modern transistors
facts: Since 2007, hafnium oxide has replaced silicon dioxide as the gate insulator in leading-edge chips.
summary: Hafnia insulating layers only a few nanometers thick made modern transistors possible.

name: Tantalum pentoxide

structure.note: One formula unit; real solid has complex chains of TaO6/TaO7 polyhedra.

bonding.summary: Ta5+ in oxygen polyhedra; highly insulating with a high dielectric constant.
bonding.electronSharing: Tantalum gives all five valence electrons toward oxygen.

facts: The thin oxide grown on tantalum powder is what stores charge in a tantalum capacitor.
summary: Ta2O5 is the insulating film inside tantalum capacitors.

name: Rhenium(VII) oxide

structure.note: Formal charges; the gas is O3Re–O–ReO3 molecules and the solid a polymer of linked ReO4 and ReO6 units.

bonding.summary: In the gas, two ReO4 tetrahedra share one oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Rhenium shares all seven valence electrons with oxygen in strong, largely covalent bonds.

uses: Making perrhenic acid and rhenium catalysts
facts: It sublimes at about 360 °C, so it can be purified by vapor transport.
summary: Re2O7 is a volatile yellow oxide used to make rhenium catalysts.

name: Silicon carbide

structure.note: Cubic 3C-SiC; many other stacking forms exist.

bonding.summary: Every Si bonded to four C and every C to four Si: a diamond-like network of two elements.
bonding.electronSharing: Silicon and carbon share electron pairs in four tetrahedral bonds, pulled toward carbon (Δχ 0.65).

formation: SiO2 + 3 C -> SiC + 2 CO (Acheson process, about 2,500 °C)
occurrence: Rare natural mineral moissanite; found in meteorites as grains older than the Sun.
facts: Some SiC grains in meteorites formed around stars that died before the Sun was born.
summary: Silicon carbide is a hard semiconductor that handles high voltages in electric vehicles.

name: Gallium arsenide

bonding.summary: Ga and As each bonded to four of the other in a zincblende lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Gallium brings three valence electrons and arsenic five; together they make four shared pairs per atom (Δχ 0.37).

formation: Ga + As -> GaAs (grown as single crystals)
facts: Electrons move about five times faster in GaAs than in silicon.
summary: GaAs is a fast semiconductor used in phones and space solar panels.

name: Gallium nitride

bonding.summary: Each Ga bonded to four N in a hexagonal wurtzite lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Gallium and nitrogen share pairs strongly pulled toward nitrogen (Δχ 1.23), giving a wide band gap that emits blue light.

facts: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics honored the invention of efficient blue GaN LEDs.
summary: GaN made blue LEDs, and therefore white LED lighting, possible.

name: Indium phosphide

bonding.summary: Zincblende lattice of In and P.
bonding.electronSharing: Indium's three and phosphorus's five valence electrons form four shared pairs per atom.

uses: Lasers and detectors for fiber-optic communication
facts: InP lasers emit at 1.3 and 1.55 µm, the wavelengths that travel farthest in glass fiber.
summary: InP lasers send light down the internet's fiber-optic cables.

name: Cadmium telluride

bonding.summary: Zincblende lattice of Cd and Te.
bonding.electronSharing: Cadmium and tellurium share pairs fairly evenly (Δχ 0.41); the band gap of 1.5 eV suits sunlight.

facts: CdTe panels are the second most common solar technology after silicon.
summary: CdTe thin films make low-cost solar panels.

name: Cadmium sulfide

bonding.summary: Wurtzite lattice of Cd and S.
bonding.electronSharing: Cadmium and sulfur share pairs pulled toward sulfur (Δχ 0.89); the 2.4 eV band gap absorbs blue light, so CdS is yellow.

uses: Buffer layer in thin-film solar cells
facts: Painters such as Monet used cadmium yellow.
summary: CdS is a bright yellow pigment and light-sensitive semiconductor.

name: Zinc oxide

bonding.summary: Each Zn tetrahedrally bonded to four O in wurtzite.
bonding.electronSharing: Zinc gives its two 4s electrons toward oxygen with strong polarity (Δχ 1.79).

uses: Varistors that protect electronics from surges
facts: ZnO is white at room temperature but turns yellow when hot.
hazards: Low toxicity; fumes cause metal fume fever.
summary: Zinc oxide protects skin from UV and helps make car tires.

name: Indium tin oxide

structure.note: Host In2O3 formula unit; about 10% of indium is replaced by tin (Sn4+), each releasing a free electron.

bonding.summary: An In2O3 lattice in which Sn4+ replaces some In3+.
bonding.electronSharing: Each Sn4+ that replaces In3+ gives one extra electron to the crystal, making it conduct like a metal while staying transparent.

formation: Sputtering In2O3 and SnO2 targets onto glass
facts: Almost every touchscreen has a layer of ITO only about 100 nm thick.
summary: ITO is a transparent conductor, the invisible wiring of touchscreens.

name: Yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO)

structure.note: Formal charges; the real crystal is a layered perovskite with CuO2 planes and CuO chains.

bonding.summary: Layers of CuO2 planes separated by Y, Ba and CuO chains.
bonding.electronSharing: Copper and oxygen share electrons in flat CuO2 sheets. Missing electrons ('holes') in those sheets pair up below 93 K and flow with zero resistance.

formation: Y2O3 + 4 BaCO3 + 6 CuO -> sintered at about 950 °C in oxygen
facts: Discovered in 1987, it was the first superconductor above the 77 K boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
summary: YBCO superconducts at 93 K, warm enough to cool with cheap liquid nitrogen.

name: Lithium cobalt oxide

structure.note: Real structure: layers of CoO2 with lithium ions between them.

bonding.summary: Layers of CoO2 sheets with Li+ ions in between that can slide in and out.
bonding.electronSharing: When the battery charges, Li+ leaves the layers and cobalt gives up an electron (Co3+ to Co4+); discharging reverses it.

uses: Cathode of lithium-ion batteries in phones and laptops
facts: John Goodenough's 1980 discovery of LiCoO2 cathodes contributed to his 2019 Nobel Prize.
hazards: Toxic; can release oxygen if overheated.
summary: LiCoO2 is the cathode in most phone and laptop batteries.
